newsitem.title: UK: Rally hears peace pleas in tense Northern Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Rally hears peace pleas in tense Northern Ireland.

text.p: As Northern Ireland held its breath on Friday fearing fresh violence, some of the maimed and bereaved of its bitter guerrilla war joined hundreds of the "silent majority" in a rally for peace in central Belfast.
"At this present time we are all on tenterhooks, not knowing what's going to happen," Protestant Yvonne Cromie told the crowd.
"The children of this country have got a death threat on their heads," Roman Catholic Maria McShane lamented.
The crowd, heads bowed, held high more than 3,000 paper cut-out figures representing the death toll of a war they fear could restart at any minute.
Both women lost a teenage son, killed by gangs of maurauding gunmen who struck terror in pro-British Protestant and Irish Catholic neighbourhoods at the height of "the Troubles".
"We still don't know why his life was taken," Cromie said. "I have lost something very, very precious," said McShane, who was badly injured in a bomb explosion 20 years ago.

Women Together, one of several inter-community groups that have struggled for years to keep alive peace hopes of people, many of them unaligned to political parties, held the rally to give a voice to the "silent majority", a spokeswoman said.

The rally coincided with the award of the Nobel Peace prize to two East Timorese independence activists. In 1976 the Nobel award was shared by Betty Williams and Mairead Corrigan, leader of the "Peace People" movement in Northern Ireland.

Hours before the rally started, a British soldier died from wounds received in the region's first IRA bomb attack for two years. His death fuelled anxiety about possible retaliatory attacks by pro-British Loyalist guerrillas.
"This rally is to encourage people to focus on the need for every individual to work towards the new society that we all want to see," said Anne Carr, one of the organisers.

"If you feed people a diet of despair, they give up hope. If you give them a diet of hope, they'll have hope," she told Reuters. "We are never going to have lasting peace unless each individual takes responsibility for achieving it."

Carr was a prime mover behind a rally in February when the Irish Republican Army resumed a bloody campaign against British rule after a 17-month truce with a bombing in London's Docklands industrial and housing redevelopment area that killed two men.
On Monday, the IRA switched their nine-month bombing campaign from mainland Britain to Northern Ireland, setting off two carbombs inside British army headquarters at Lisburn, south of Belfast.
For the province's beleagured community the blast and its shattering effects have revived nightmarish memories of a war that most people hoped had been consigned to history.
Loyalist guerrillas, who killed Catholic Irish nationalists in a bid to safeguard British rule, are reported to be meeting soon to decide whether to end a two-year truce and retaliate.

"I plead with the Loyalists, please continue with your ceasefire. I beg and I plead with the IRA, please start another ceasefire," McShane said, before a children's choir chanted "Give Peace A Chance". There was then a minute's silence.

In front of Belfast City Hall, where late last year U.S. President Bill Clinton addressed thousands of Catholics and Protestants, applauding their peace efforts, the thousand-strong crowd said it wanted to banish all violence.

Mark Kelly, who lost his legs in a no-warning guerrilla bomb explosion 18 years ago, told them: "This is a time to let the governments, the politicians and the warmongers know, that we want no more death and no more war.
